source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Encourage vigorous walking, warm the arms and legs first, and reassess after the client becomes more alert.","B":"Handle gently, prevent further heat loss, actively rewarm the trunk, and monitor the cardiac rhythm.","C":"Massage the extremities vigorously and apply peripheral heat to move warm blood toward the core.","D":"Apply unmonitored direct high heat to numb skin and delay cardiac monitoring until rewarming is complete."}}
source_row.rationale: A core temperature of 31°C with altered mental status is clinically significant hypothermia. Care includes gentle handling, prevention of further heat loss, active external rewarming focused on the trunk, and cardiac monitoring because dysrhythmias can occur. Option B is correct. Vigorous exercise, extremity massage, and uncontrolled direct heat are unsafe.
source_row.source_detail: Moderate hypothermia/management: temperatures about 28-32°C are moderate; handle patients gently because of dysrhythmia risk, prevent further heat loss, use active external rewarming for moderate hypothermia with heat directed to the trunk, and monitor cardiac status. Current StatPearls Hypothermia entry live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: acute/complex alterations, emergency response and pathophysiologic adaptation. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
source_row.stem: A client exposed to cold has a core temperature of 31°C (87.8°F), confusion, and slowed responses. Which management principle is most appropriate?
